Dolge Orlick was working with us the next day when I reminded Joe that I had a half-day off. He didn't say anything right away because he and Joe were busy with a piece of hot metal, and I was working the bellows. But later, he leaned on his hammer and said, 'Hey, boss, you're not going to play favorites, are you? If Pip gets a half-day off, I should get one too.' I think he was about twenty-five, but he always talked about himself like he was an old man. Joe asked him, 'What would you do with a half-day off?' Orlick replied, 'What's Pip going to do with it? I can do the same things he can.' Joe said, 'Pip's going into town.' Orlick shot back, 'Well, I'm going into town too. Just because Pip can go doesn't mean I shouldn't be able to.' Joe told him not to get angry, but Orlick just grumbled, 'I'll get angry if I want to. Some people think they're so special just because they get to go into town.' The boss didn't want to deal with Orlick when he was in a bad mood, so Orlick went back to work, pulled out a red-hot bar, and pretended to stab me with it. He swung it around my head, put it on the anvil, and started hammering away, like he was pounding out his frustration. Finally, when he'd cooled down a bit, he said, 'Okay, boss, I'm ready to talk now.' Joe asked him if he was feeling better, and Orlick just grunted, 'Yeah, I'm fine.' Joe said, 'You usually do your job just like everyone else, so let's just give everyone the half-day off.' My sister had been standing outside, listening in without saying a word - she was always snooping around and eavesdropping. As soon as she heard the decision, she looked in through one of the windows.

He lived with a man who took care of a sluice out on the marshes. It was as if he was always thinking that it was strange he didn't have any thoughts. This man, a skilled worker, didn't like me. When I was little, he told me that the Devil lived in a dark corner of the blacksmith shop and that he knew the Devil well. “Biddy,” I said, after swearing her to secrecy, “I have a strong desire to become a gentleman.” “Oh, I wouldn’t, if I were you,” she replied. “I don’t think it would be the right choice.” “Biddy,” I said, with a hint of sternness, “I have specific reasons for wanting to be a gentleman.” “You know what’s best for you, Pip,” she said, “but don’t you think you’re happier as you are?” “Biddy,” I exclaimed, with growing impatience, “I am not happy at all as I am. I have never taken to my trade or my life since I was apprenticed. Don’t be ridiculous.” “Was I being ridiculous?” Biddy asked, quietly raising an eyebrow. “I apologize if I was; I didn’t mean to be. I only want what’s best for you, and for you to be content.” “Well, then, understand once and for all,” I said, “that I will never be content, or anything but miserable, unless I can lead a very different life from the one I lead now.” “That’s a shame,” Biddy said, shaking her head with a sorrowful expression. I had often thought the same, and in my internal struggle, I was half inclined to shed tears of frustration and distress when Biddy echoed my sentiment. I told her she was right, and I knew it was regrettable, but it was unavoidable. “If I could have settled into my life,” I said to Biddy, pulling at the short grass nearby, much like I used to pull my feelings out of my hair and kick them away, “if I could have been even half as fond of the forge as I was when I was little, I know it would have been much better for me. You, Joe, and I would have wanted for nothing, and Joe and I might have even become partners when I finished my apprenticeship. I might have even grown up to be worthy of your company, and we might have sat on this very bank on a fine Sunday, as very different people. I would have been good enough for you, wouldn’t I, Biddy?” Biddy sighed as she gazed out at the ships sailing by, and replied, “Yes, I’m not overly particular.” It didn’t sound like a compliment, but I knew she meant well. “Instead of that,” I said, pulling up more grass and chewing on a blade or two, “look at how I’m doing. I’m dissatisfied, uncomfortable, and—what would it matter to me, being coarse and common, if no one had pointed it out?” Biddy turned to face me, looking at me more intently than she had at the ships. “That wasn’t a very kind or truthful thing to say,” she remarked, directing her gaze back to the ships. “Who said it?” I was taken aback, as I had spoken without thinking. Mr. Jaggers said, “First, you should acquire some new clothes, not your work clothes. Let us say this day next week. You will need some money.” He pulled out a long purse with great composure, counted out twenty guineas on the table, and slid them over to me. This was the first time he had moved his leg from the chair. As he sat astride the chair, swinging his purse and eyeing Joe, he asked, “Well, Joseph Gargery, you seem astonished?” Joe replied, “I am!” in a very resolute manner. Mr. Jaggers reminded him, “It was understood that you wanted nothing for yourself, remember?” Joe confirmed, “It was understood, and it still is, and it always will be the same.” Mr. Jaggers swung his purse, saying, “But what if my instructions were to give you a gift as compensation?” Joe asked, “Compensation for what?” Mr. Jaggers replied, “For the loss of Pip's services.” Joe placed his hand on my shoulder with a gentle touch, like a woman's. I have often thought of him as a steam-hammer, capable of crushing a man or handling an eggshell with care, due to his combination of strength and gentleness. Joe said, “Pip is welcome to go freely with his services, to honour and fortune, as no words can express. But if you think money can compensate me for the loss of the little child who came to the forge and was my best friend...” Oh, dear good Joe, whom I was so ready to leave and so ungrateful to, I see you again with your muscular blacksmith's arm before your eyes, your broad chest heaving, and your voice fading away. Oh, dear good faithful tender Joe, I feel the loving tremble of your hand on my arm, as solemnly this day as if it had been the rustle of an angel's wing. I encouraged Joe at the time, lost in the complexities of my future fortunes, unable to retrace the paths we had walked together. I begged Joe to be comforted, reminding him that we had always been the best of friends and would continue to be so. Joe wiped his eyes with his wrist, as if trying to gouge himself, but said no more. Mr. Jaggers watched this exchange, seeming to view Joe as a simpleton and me as his caretaker. When it was over, he said, weighing the purse in his hand, “Now, Joseph Gargery, I warn you this is your last chance. No half-measures with me. If you mean to accept a gift that I have been instructed to give you, speak out, and you shall have it. If, on the other hand, you mean to say...” But to his great surprise, Joe suddenly turned on him, displaying every intention of engaging in a fierce fight.

And yet I couldn't,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising from his seat once more, “look at One—and also toast One—without once more expressing—May I—_may_ I—?” I gave him permission, and he shook hands with me again, drained his glass, and turned it over. I did the same, and the wine went straight to my head, as if I had turned myself upside down before drinking. Mr. Pumblechook served me the liver wing and the best slice of tongue, taking little care of himself in comparison. “Ah, poultry, poultry! You never thought,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl on the platter, “when you were a young bird, what lay in store for you. You never imagined you would be a meal under this humble roof for someone like—Call it a weakness, if you will,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “but may I? _may_ I—?” It was becoming unnecessary to repeat the form of saying he might, so he proceeded at once. I was amazed he didn't hurt himself with my knife, considering how often he did it. After eating for a while, he continued, “And your sister, who had the honour of raising you by hand! It's a sad picture to think that she's no longer capable of fully understanding the honour. May—” I saw he was about to ask again, and I stopped him. “We'll drink to her health,” I said. “Ah!” exclaimed Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely relaxed in admiration, “that's how you know them, sir!” (I didn't know who Sir was, but it wasn't me, and there was no one else present); “that's how you know the noble-minded, sir! Ever forgiving and ever affable. To a common person, it might seem like repetition—but _may_ I—?” When he had finished, he sat down and drank to my sister's health. “Let us never be blind,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “to her temper flaws, but it's to be hoped she meant well.” Around this time, I started to notice that he was getting red in the face, while I felt my face was on fire from the wine. I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was overjoyed that I had chosen him. I explained that I wanted to avoid being seen in the village, and he praised my decision. He implied that he was the only one worthy of my trust, and—in short, might he? Then he asked me if I remembered our childhood games with numbers and how we had gone together to have me apprenticed, and, in effect, how he had always been my favourite friend and chosen companion? Even if I had drunk ten times as much wine as I had, I would have known that he had never been that close to me, and I would have rejected the idea in my heart. Yet, despite this, I felt convinced that I had misjudged him and that he was a sensible, practical, and kind person.

And yet I couldn't,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “look at you and raise a glass without saying it again - may I, may I? I gave him the okay, and he shook my hand again, downed his drink, and turned his glass over. I did the same, and if I had flipped myself over before drinking, the wine couldn't have hit me harder. Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the best part of the liver and the top slice of tongue - none of the lower-quality cuts now - and didn't worry too much about his own serving. 'Oh, poultry, poultry!' Mr. Pumblechook exclaimed, talking to the food on his plate. 'You never thought, when you were young, what was in store for you. You had no idea you'd end up being served under this humble roof for someone like... Call it a weakness if you want,' said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, 'but may I, may I?' It was getting pointless to keep giving him permission, so he just went ahead. I have no idea how he managed to do it so many times without accidentally stabbing himself with my knife. 'And your sister,' he continued, after eating for a bit, 'who had the honor of raising you by hand. It's sad to think that she's not fully aware of the honor she's given you. May...' I saw him getting ready to ask again, so I cut him off. 'Let's drink to her health,' I said. 'Ah!' cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely impressed. 'That's how you treat people with class, sir!' - though I have no idea who 'sir' was, since it wasn't me and there was no one else there. 'That's how you know someone with a noble mind, sir - always forgiving and always friendly. To a regular person, it might seem like I'm repeating myself, but... may I?' After he did it again, he sat back down and drank to my sister's health. 'Let's not ignore her flaws,' said Mr. Pumblechook, 'but hopefully, she meant well.' Around this time, I started to notice that Mr. Pumblechook's face was getting red, and as for me, I felt like my whole face was burning from the wine. I told Mr. Pumblechook that I wanted my new clothes sent to his house, and he was over the moon that I was giving him such an honor. I explained that I wanted to avoid drawing attention to myself in the village, and he thought it was a great idea. He implied that he was the only one worthy of my trust, and... well, might he? Then he asked me if I remembered the times we played with numbers as kids and how we went to get me set up as an apprentice, and basically, how he had always been my favorite person and closest friend. Even if I had ten times as much wine as I did, I would have known that he never actually felt that way about me, and deep down, I would have rejected the idea. Still, for some reason, I felt convinced that I had misjudged him and that he was actually a sensible, practical, and kind guy.

Mr. Pumblechook stood up again and said, 'I'd like to make a toast to someone special. May I?' I told him it was okay, and we shook hands. Then we drank our wine. I felt the wine go straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook helped me get some food, giving me the best pieces. He didn't take much for himself. 'You didn't know what would happen to you when you were young,' he said to the food. 'You didn't know you'd be eaten here today.' He got up again and said, 'May I?' I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook's face was getting red, and I felt my face burning from the wine. I told him I wanted to send my new clothes to his house, and he was thrilled. I discovered that Wemmick was the clerk in the adjacent room. As he stepped out, another clerk was summoned from upstairs to take his place, and I accompanied him into the street after bidding farewell to my guardian. We encountered a new group of people lingering outside, but Wemmick effortlessly navigated through them by stating calmly yet firmly, 'I assure you, it's pointless; he won't engage with any of you,' and we soon cleared a path and continued on our way side by side.

As we walked, I took the opportunity to observe Mr. Wemmick in the daylight. I found him to be a somewhat austere man, slightly below average height, with a wooden face whose features seemed to have been roughly hewn with a blunt instrument. There were a few marks on his face that could have been dimples if the material had been more pliable and the tool more refined, but instead, they appeared as mere indentations. The instrument had attempted to create a few of these decorative touches above his nose but had abandoned the effort without smoothing them out. I surmised that he was a bachelor, given the worn state of his linen, and he seemed to have experienced numerous losses, as evidenced by the multiple mourning rings he wore, in addition to a brooch depicting a lady and a weeping willow beside a tomb with an urn. I also noticed that several rings and seals hung from his watch-chain, as if he were heavily burdened with memories of departed friends. His eyes sparkled - small, sharp, and black - and his lips were thin, wide, and mottled. To the best of my knowledge, he had possessed these features for forty to fifty years.

'Had you never been to London before?' Mr. Wemmick inquired of me.

'No,' I replied.

'I, too, was once new to this city,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'It's strange to think about now.'

'Are you well acquainted with London now?' I asked.

'Oh, yes,' said Mr. Wemmick. 'I'm familiar with its ways.'

'Is it a particularly wicked place?' I asked, more out of a desire to make conversation than to gain insight.

'You can be deceived, robbed, or murdered in London,' he said. 'However, there are plenty of people elsewhere who would do the same to you.'

'If there's ill will between you and them,' I added, attempting to soften the statement.

'Oh, I don't know about ill will,' Mr. Wemmick responded. 'There isn't much of that about. They'll do it if there's something to be gained.'

'That makes it worse,' I said.

'Do you think so?' Mr. Wemmick replied. 'I'd say it's much the same.'

He wore his hat at the back of his head and gazed straight ahead, walking with a self-assured air as if nothing in the streets warranted his attention. His mouth seemed to be perpetually frozen in a mechanical smile, giving him a somewhat artificial appearance. We had reached the top of Holborn Hill before I realized that this was merely a facade, and he wasn't actually smiling at all.

'Do you know where Mr. Matthew Pocket resides?' I asked Mr. Wemmick.

'Yes,' he replied, nodding in a particular direction. 'He lives in Hammersmith, to the west of London.'

'Is that far?'

The gusts had been so intense that they had stripped the lead from the roofs of tall buildings in town, and in the countryside, trees had been uprooted and windmill sails had been carried away. Reports from the coast had been grim, with accounts of shipwrecks and loss of life. The day that had just ended had been the most severe, with violent blasts of rain accompanying the fierce winds. As I sat down to read, the alterations that had been made to the Temple since then were not yet in place, and it still had a somewhat isolated character, exposed as it was to the river. Our home was at the top of the last house, and the wind rushing up the river that night shook the house violently, much like the sound of cannon fire or the crashing of waves. When the rain lashed against the windows, I felt as though I might have imagined myself in a storm-battered lighthouse, the windows rocking back and forth. Occasionally, the smoke would billow down the chimney, as if it too were reluctant to venture out into the tempestuous night. When I opened the doors and peered down the staircase, I found that the lamps had been extinguished by the wind, and when I cautiously approached the windows, shielding my face with my hands, I saw that the lamps in the courtyard and on the bridges and shore were also being buffeted by the gale, while the coal fires on the barges were being swept away like glowing embers in the rain. I had placed my watch on the table, intending to stop reading at eleven o'clock. As I closed my book, the sound of Saint Paul's and the numerous church clocks in the City striking the hour filled the air, though the wind distorted the sound. I was lost in thought, pondering the way the wind was assaulting the clocks, when I heard the sound of footsteps on the stairs. When evaluating an author's merit and determining their place among our most revered figures, we are entitled to assess them from our own perspective and measure them against our own standards. However, in evaluating the power displayed in their works, we must consider their own intentions and compare their creations to their ideal, noting what is lacking. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the objectives of art, as he believes the primary goal is to create Beauty, although our disagreement may stem from differing definitions of this term. Nonetheless, in our discussion of his writings, we will adhere to his own standards. The realm of the god of song is accessible from all sides, and there is ample space for all who bring offerings or seek guidance. In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his skill primarily in the realm that lies between the boundaries of probability and the realm of superstition and unreality. He possesses a rare combination of faculties, blending the ability to influence the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and a meticulous attention to detail that overlooks nothing. Both of these qualities are, in fact, natural consequences of the dominant characteristic of his mind, which is analysis. This analytical mind enables the artist to focus on the intended effect, making all elements subordinate to the central goal. Even his mysterious elements are subject to mathematical precision in his own mind, where the unknown quantity is always known. When he creates a picture, he is aware of the chemical properties of all the colors he uses, and although some of his figures may seem vague or formless, their outlines are as clear to him as a geometric diagram. This is why Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism, which immerses itself in mystery and allows it to permeate all thoughts. In contrast, Mr. Poe approaches his subject from the outside, analyzing, dissecting, and observing with a serene eye the intricate mechanisms at work. This analytical tendency balances his poetic inclinations, granting him the patience to be meticulous and infuse his most fanciful creations with a sense of reality. He is particularly skilled at portraying monomania, dissecting the subtle roots of these mental afflictions with great power. He also excels at evoking images of horror, often conveying a sense of terrible doubt through subtle hints, leaving the imagination to complete the picture, a task for which it is uniquely suited. As it is said, 'much imaginary work was there; Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind, That for Achilles' image stood his spear Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.'

My primary objective is to establish a magazine, to be titled 'The Stylus,' but it would be of little value to me if it were not entirely under my control, free from the influence of a publisher. To achieve this, I intend to create a journal that is truly my own in every aspect. With this goal in mind, I must secure a list of at least five hundred subscribers before launching the magazine; I have already gathered nearly two hundred. I plan to travel to the South and West to meet with my personal and literary acquaintances, including old college and West Point friends, to see what support I can garner. To raise the necessary funds for the initial step, I propose to deliver a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, February 3rd, and to avoid any potential controversy, my topic will not be literary in nature. I have chosen a broad and universal subject: 'The Universe.' Having presented you with the facts of the matter, I leave the rest to your discretion and generosity. I am deeply grateful. Your friend always, EDGAR A. POE. Although these letters are brief and hastily written, they demonstrate the presence of qualities often denied to Mr. Poe, such as humility, perseverance, and a capacity for genuine and grateful friendship. These traits were undoubtedly characteristic of him when he was sane, and they have consistently been our experience of him throughout our five- or six-year friendship. It is easier to believe what we have personally witnessed than what we have only heard, and so we remember him with admiration and respect; the descriptions of him during periods of moral insanity seem to us like portraits of a man we have only known in health, painted during times of sickness. However, there is another, more poignant and compelling evidence of the goodness in Edgar A. Poe. To reveal this, we must delicately lift the veil that shields the grief and refinement of those living in poverty, but we believe it is justified if it can help to illuminate the poet's memory, and it may also serve a more immediate and necessary purpose in the aftermath of his death. Our first knowledge of Mr. Poe's move to this city came when a lady introduced herself as the mother of his wife and visited us, seeking employment for him. She explained that he was ill, her daughter was a confirmed invalid, and their circumstances were such that she felt compelled to take action. The lady's countenance, radiant with a selfless devotion to a life of hardship and sorrowful tenderness, her gentle and mournful voice, her refined yet understated manners, and her appreciative mention of her son's abilities, all revealed a truly angelic presence, one of those extraordinary women who rise above adversity. It was a difficult fate that she was struggling to overcome, as Mr. Poe's writing, though meticulous and refined, was not well-suited to the popular taste and therefore not well-rewarded.

In approximately four and a half hours, the balloon was sufficiently inflated, so I attached the car and loaded all my equipment, including the condensing apparatus, a substantial amount of water, and a generous supply of provisions like pemmican, which is rich in nutrients despite its compact size. I also placed a pair of pigeons and a cat in the car. As daybreak was approaching, I deemed it time to depart. While pretending to pick up a lit cigar I had dropped, I discreetly ignited the slow match that protruded slightly from one of the smaller casks. This action went unnoticed by the three men nearby, and I quickly jumped into the car, cut the cord that tied me to the ground, and was pleased to find that I ascended effortlessly, carrying 175 pounds of leaden ballast with ease and capable of carrying just as much more. However, I had barely reached a height of 50 yards when a violent hurricane of fire, smoke, sulfur, and debris erupted beneath me, causing my heart to sink and filling me with unbridled terror. I realized too late that I had overestimated the situation, and the full consequences of the explosion were still to come. In an instant, I felt my blood rushing to my temples, followed by a deafening concussion that seemed to tear the sky apart. Later, when I had time to reflect, I attributed the explosion's intense violence to my position directly above it, but in the moment, my only concern was survival. The balloon initially collapsed, then expanded furiously, spinning around with terrifying speed before hurling me over the car's rim, leaving me dangling at a great height, upside down, with my face outward, suspended by a slender cord that had become entangled around my left foot. The horror of my situation was indescribable - I gasped for air, my body convulsed with fear, my eyes felt like they were being torn from their sockets, and a wave of nausea washed over me before I lost consciousness. I have no idea how long I remained in this state, but when I partially regained my senses, I found the balloon at an immense height above a vast expanse of ocean, with no sign of land in sight, and the day breaking on the horizon.
